Renewing MyMVA
UX Case Study

Renewing
MyMVA.

A mobile redesign of Maryland's Motor Vehicle Administration website. The goal was simple to say and hard to do: make renewing a license or booking an appointment feel like less of an errand.

RoleUX / UI Design
PlatformMobile Web
DeliverableFigma Prototype
01

The site today

Nobody opens MVA.Maryland.gov for fun. You're there to renew a license, book a road test, or handle something that's already a hassle, and on mobile it still feels like a desktop site that got shrunk down rather than one built for a phone. Dense text blocks, a long undifferentiated menu, and small tap targets make it slow to find the one thing you came to do.

The MVA website, while functional, could benefit from a more modern design that makes it easier to use, faster, and simpler to navigate, especially on mobile. A smoother, more user-friendly experience would make services more efficient and help build trust and satisfaction with users.

The homepage isn't the whole story, though. A level deeper, MVA's own site already reaches for some of the same ideas a redesign would: bold service icons, a red "I want to..." menu, alert carousels, even employee spotlight stories. These are all existing MVA pages, not something I designed. The raw material for a better mobile experience is already there. It's just scattered across separate pages instead of working together from one clear entry point.

02

Research and direction

I started close to home, looking at how other states handle their own Motor Vehicle Administration sites, and paying attention to which ones were actually accessible: readable contrast, clear focus states, tap targets that didn't demand precision. Then I looked further out, at booking apps, course platforms, and dealership sites, for how they handle the same underlying problem as MVA's: a long list of possible actions that needs to resolve into one clear next step. A few ideas kept showing up and became the working principles for the redesign.

✓

Feature large, bold buttons for key services so users can immediately identify and access the most commonly used ones.

✓

Use contrasting colors for important actions like appointments, renewals, or payments, paired with icons so tasks are easy to scan.

✓

Organize the main navigation with clear categories, using drop-downs to group related services under each one.

✓

Opt for a minimalist layout with generous whitespace, so the page feels less cluttered and easier to navigate.

03

From wireframe to screen

Before touching color, I blocked out the structure: what sits above the fold, how many actions the homepage can reasonably hold, and where a search bar earns its place. Six quick low-fidelity passes settled the skeleton the later screens were built on.

04

First pass: staying close to home

The first draft kept MVA's navy, but softened the agency's brighter yellow into a creamier, warmer tone, and tightened the login-first structure around a clear "I want to..." menu of popular transactions, so a returning visitor could get to a renewal in one tap instead of hunting through a menu.

Home & login
Resources & news
05

The final design

The finished design keeps MVA's own blue, red, and gold, the same palette the agency's site already uses well on pages like its "I want to..." menu, and applies it consistently from the homepage down. Services are grouped into a scannable grid up top, with the full list still one tap away underneath for anyone who needs it. This is a screen recording of the working prototype.

This was a personal exercise in taking a real, high-stakes government site and asking what it would look like if the mobile experience came first instead of last. Some of the best raw material was already sitting on MVA's own site, just waiting to be pulled together into one clear entry point.
